title: Spain's first general strike in 14 years hits ports and car plants over rents and wages
content:
Spain staged its first general strike in 14 years on Wednesday, as workers and tenants walked out over soaring housing costs and wages that have not kept up. The 24-hour stoppage disrupted ports and car factories less than three weeks before a snap general election.

In brief
  • The strike ran under the slogan "Wages, housing and prices" and was backed by Spain's two largest unions, CCOO and UGT.
  • Unions said participation reached 90% at ports and in the car industry, with full stoppages at Volkswagen's Navarre plant and at SEAT.
  • Industrial electricity demand fell 25.6%, Euronews reported; employers called the strike a failure.
  • Police reported at least 115 arrests nationwide, mainly during evening clashes in Barcelona and Madrid, Reuters reported.

The economic hit

Unions and employers gave opposite verdicts. One measurable sign of disruption was a 25.6% drop in industrial electricity demand, according to Euronews.

SectorParticipation claimed by unions
Ports (notably Valencia, Algeciras)90%
Car industry90%
Meat industry85%
Waste collection82%

Source: CCOO and UGT, via Euronews.

Madrid's metro, running a minimum service, carried 21% fewer passengers at 7 a.m.

80%
Rise in Spanish rents over the past decade, while home prices climbed 63%, The Guardian reported.

Why people walked out

The average rent of €1,176 ($1,315) equals about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain, Reuters reported. The Tenants' Union, which spearheaded the strike, said more than 3 million people joined demonstrations.

Turnout estimates diverged widely. In Madrid the Tenants' Union counted more than half a million marchers, while the central government's office put it at 120,000. In Barcelona, organisers said 400,000 and city police 55,000.

Politics weeks before the vote

Spain holds a general election on Nov. 29. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called it after right-wing parties defeated emergency housing legislation, The Guardian reported.

Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo warned the unions may have made a "historic mistake". UGT leader Pepe Álvarez replied that whoever governs "will have to listen to the people".

Police recorded 1,500 incidents nationwide, Euronews said. It was the eighth general strike since Spain returned to democracy in the late 1970s.
